title: Love without measure (Bernard, On Loving God)
hookLine: the reason for loving God is God; the measure is without measure
tomorrow: can wanting something already be a way of looking for it?

lines: A MEASURE THAT IS NO MEASURE.
cards: Screen-time reports, step counts, a budget app: we measure almost everything now. So did a cardinal named Haimeric, who sent a monk two questions: why should God be loved, and how much?

Bernard, the abbot of Clairvaux, answered the second with a sentence that sounds like a riddle: the measure of loving God is to love without measure. A measure that is no measure. What could that mean?

teach.b: First, the reason. Before the how much, Bernard answers the why, near the start of On Loving God: the reason for loving God is God himself. Not a reward, not a fear, not a deal.
Second, the riddle. Every other love in a life gets weighed: time, attention, what's left at the end of the day.

teach.h: NOT A BIG NUMBER: NO NUMBER.
teach.b: Bernard's measure isn't a big number. It's no number. It's a rule against the scale itself.
Bernard leans on the First Letter of John, which in the Douay-Rheims says: "Let us therefore love God, because God first hath loved us." Love begins on God's side; ours is an answer.
And an answer to a gift with no ceiling can't have one either. Fourth, the fairness.
Nothing is more just, Bernard says, than loving the one who loved first, and nothing does the lover more good.
Later in the book he traces love growing in stages, from loving yourself for your own sake toward loving even yourself for God's sake.
But it all starts with that sentence: no reason but God, and no measure but none.

how: Catholics honor Bernard of Clairvaux as a saint and Doctor of the Church; On Loving God is read in monasteries and by people learning to pray.

o: giving God a fixed share of your time
a love so calm it never asks anything
loving God with no scale and no limit

games.q: love without measure — tap the pairs.

s: Bernard says to love God mainly for the reward of heaven
the reason for loving God, he says, is God himself.
Bernard leans on 1 John: God first hath loved us
love starts on God's side, and ours is an answer.
Bernard wrote On Loving God without anyone asking
it answers questions sent to him by a cardinal, Haimeric.

games.q: a friend says she'll love God "about ten percent, like a tithe." Bernard overhears. what's his reply?
o: the measure of loving God is to love without measure.
ten percent is right: that's the amount scripture sets.
make it half, so the rest of life stays in balance.
games.why: Bernard refuses the scale itself: the reason for loving God is God, and the measure is without measure. God loved first, and the answer has no ceiling.

practice: Count on your fingers the things you've been given that you never earned or measured out: a breath, a face, a meal someone cooked, this morning.
Keep counting past the point where it feels like enough, and past the point where you run out of fingers. Rest at the end in John's line: God first hath loved us.

wordCard.voice: Love without measure. Bernard's one-sentence answer to a cardinal: the reason is God himself, and the amount has no scale at all.

orig.note: Latin for without measure: Bernard's answer to how much God should be loved.

carryVoice: Keep this: without measure, because God loved first and the answer has no ceiling. Back tomorrow.
